content.text:
I read both against the tone notes (short, plain, focused on yield and safety of principal, for a retired yield-watcher and a household budgeter).

**Clarity — Letter A.** A breaks the quarter into labeled sections and, critically, translates the two pieces of jargon a non-specialist would stumble on: it defines duration ("a measure of how much the value of the bonds moves when interest rates move") and explains the agency trim in cause-and-effect terms ("can be called away early by the issuer, and the extra yield... no longer seemed worth accepting that uncertainty"). It also ties duration back to the account's purpose. B leaves "time-weighted total return," "strategic roll," "callable agency spreads were too tight," and "duration" unglossed, and packs all three portfolio actions into one dense block. B also buries the required yield-to-maturity disclosure at the bottom, far from the 3.72% figure it qualifies, where a reader is least likely to connect the two; A places it immediately after the number.

**Tone — Letter A.** A is plain, direct, and ends with a concrete offer ("please call if you would like to walk through the individual rungs or the maturity schedule"), which suits a client who follows yields daily and will want the detail. B drifts corporate and mildly promotional — "I am pleased to share," "a change... that will benefit your account," "reflects our commitment to providing high-quality service at a sustainable cost as our fixed-income ladders operate under their own efficient schedule." A fee cut sells itself; the marketing gloss reads as spin to a budget-running reader. B also repeatedly says "our ladder" and "our benchmark," subtly centering the firm rather than the household, and omits the firm letterhead, date, and any invitation to follow up.

B's one genuine advantage is naming safety of principal up front, which matches the mandate. That isn't enough to offset the denser prose, the stranded disclosure, and the promotional register.

It also places the required yield-to-maturity disclosure immediately after the 3.72% figure it qualifies. Letter B compresses performance, the roll, duration, and the agency trim into dense blocks and leaves "time-weighted total return," "strategic roll," "callable agency spreads were too tight," and "duration" unexplained, and it strands the disclosure at the foot of the letter away from the number it modifies. On tone, A is plain and direct and closes with a concrete offer to walk through the rungs and maturity schedule, which fits a retired client who checks yields daily and a spouse running the budget. B drifts into corporate and mildly promotional register ("I am pleased to share," "a change that will benefit your account," "our commitment to providing high-quality service at a sustainable cost," "efficient schedule") — a fee cut needs no selling — and repeatedly says "our ladder"/"our benchmark," centering the firm over the household; it also drops the firm letterhead, date, and any invitation to follow up. B's only real edge is naming safety of principal up front, which does match the mandate, but that does not offset the denser prose, misplaced disclosure, and promotional gloss. Judgment is on clarity and tone only, not length or accuracy.
